This approach preserves both the diversity and the expected dependencies that influence vehicle type and operation. 4.2 Modeling Limitations The modeled EV charging energy may not always align with the driving demand, as it is constrained by the charging schedule and charger type. Different combinations of EV-related inputs can thus lead to a discrepancy between charging demand and charging availability. This approach can result in reduced charging energy, which is quantified with a custom output variable “unmet driving hours”, in which the EV is scheduled to be in use but does not have the required SOC to complete its driving hours. Unmet driving hours are seen in larger proportions in dwelling units with L1 chargers that lack the higher power input of L2 chargers, and charge mostly at home. Section 5 includes figures of the prominence of unmet driving hours in this measure. Unmet driving hours can be an important metric when designing vehicle and charger adoption scenarios. Input combinations with a higher number of unmet driving hours may be less realistic and, as a result, may be given less weight in scenario design. We assume a direct relationship between home occupancy and driving/charging events, which results in similar daily schedules throughout the year, with distinct patterns for weekdays and weekends. While this simplifies modeling, it may underpredict or overpredict individual charging or discharging events, as real-world behavior is more variable. Similarly, we apply the “fraction charged at home” input directly to the discharging power, reducing charging loads evenly across the year. While this might be realistic for some drivers who split their charging between home and other locations, others may instead scale their number of at-home charging events, where only certain days are used to charge at home.
